title: The must-know troublemaker verbs
goal: Gather the most common irregular verbs in one place, then use them to express obligation and ability.
bekal: telling *saber* and *conhecer* apart — two words for "know"

notes: ⚠️ **Saber and conhecer both mean "know", and they can't replace each other.** *Saber* is for **information and skills**: *sei o endereço*, *sei nadar*, *sei que ele mora aqui*. *Conhecer* is for **being acquainted with people, places or works**: *conheço a Carla*, *conheço São Paulo*, *conheço esse filme*. A way to remember it: *saber* answers "what", *conhecer* answers "who/where". English uses one word, "know", for both, so this distinction is entirely new.

**Tem que — the most Brazilian way to say "must".** Literally "has that". *Você tem que ir* = "you have to go" — the same idea as English "have to". The formal *tem de* is also correct but almost never heard in Brazil. And once again, the verb after it stays in the base form.

**Dá para — an expression with no direct equivalent.** *Dá para pagar no cartão?* literally "does it give for paying by card?", means "can you pay by card?". *Dá* is for general possibility, not a person's ability: *Não dá* = "it can't be done, no way". It's one of the most used expressions in Brazil and one of the least taught.
**Que isso!** literally "what this!", is the typical reply to over-the-top thanks — roughly "oh, come on, no big deal". It's in the same family as *imagina!* from unit 8.
**Nem** means "not even": *nem sempre* (not always), *nem sei* (I don't even know), *nem vem* (don't even start). This little word pops up constantly in fast conversation.

grammars.title: Seven must-know irregular verbs
body: The odd one out is almost always **the "I" form**. The other four rows are usually regular, so memorize the second column and the rest follows.
after: ⚠️ *Fazer* is the busiest verb in Portuguese. Besides "make/do", it's used for weather (*faz frio* = it's cold), time passed (*faz dois anos* = it's been two years), and nearly any activity (*fazer compras* = to go shopping, *fazer aniversário* = to have a birthday).
**Pronunciation to watch:** *faço* = FAH-soo, *vejo* = VAY-zhoo, *venho* = VAY-nyoo, *digo* = JEE-goo, *ponho* = POH-nyoo. They all use sounds you already know from the pronunciation chapter.
*Pôr* is the only Portuguese verb whose base form carries an accent — to tell it apart from the preposition *por* ("by, through"). They sound exactly the same.

grammars.title: Obligation and possibility
body: Four formulas that cover nearly every "must", "need" and "can" sentence. All are followed by a verb in the base form.
after: ⚠️ **Poder and saber can both be translated "can", but they mean different things.** *Posso nadar* = "I'm allowed to swim" (permission) or "I'm able to right now". *Sei nadar* = "I can swim" (I have the skill). For learned skills — swimming, driving, playing guitar, speaking a language — always use *saber*.
**Precisar needs *de* before a noun**, but not before a verb: *preciso **de** dinheiro* (I need money) but *preciso ir* (I need to go). The same pattern as *gostar* from unit 6.

grammars.title: -ir verbs that change their vowel
body: A small group of -ir verbs changes the vowel in the stem **only in the "I" form**. The other four rows are normal.
after: The pattern: **e** becomes **i**, and **o** becomes **u**, only for *eu*. The last row misbehaves the other way round — *subir* changes its *você* form instead.
*Sinto muito* means "I'm so sorry" or "my condolences" — one of those phrases worth knowing before you need it.

English
rows: What do you do (for a living)?

blocks.text: ⚠️ *O que você faz?* has two meanings depending on tone: "what's your job?" or "what are you doing?". To avoid confusion, Brazilians often spell it out: *O que você faz da vida?* for work, *O que você tá fazendo?* for what's happening right now.
⚠️ Unlike English, Portuguese **uses no article** for jobs after *ser*: *Eu sou professor*, not *eu sou um professor*.
*Motorista* and *estudante* end in **-a** and **-e** but can be male or female; only the article changes (*o motorista* / *a motorista*). This is the rule from unit 2 in action.

items: What time is it? → *Que horas são?*
It's half past seven → *São sete e meia*
I wake up at six in the morning → *Eu acordo às seis da manhã*
The class starts at ten → *A aula começa às dez*
I go to sleep at midnight → *Eu durmo à meia-noite*
